intro: Beyond the Milky Way: galaxies of two great families, nuclei that outshine their whole galaxy from a region the size of the Solar System, jets that seem to move faster than light, and clusters filled with $10^8$ K gas. Radiation processes (synchrotron, bremsstrahlung) are the tools for reading all of them.

encounters.title: Spirals and ellipticals: the Hubble sequence

blocks.html: Hubble's tuning fork: ellipticals E0 (round) to E7 (flattened) on the handle; then S0 (lenticular, disk without arms) at the fork; then two prongs, normal spirals Sa → Sb → Sc and barred spirals SBa → SBc, with smaller bulges and more open, clumpier arms towards c. Irregulars off the end. It is a classification, not an evolutionary sequence.

Ellipticals vs spirals (HS24 winter Q5 asks for three): morphology (smooth ellipsoid vs disk + bulge + arms); dynamics (random motions vs rotation); colour (red vs blue); stellar population (old, no star formation vs young, active star formation); gas (little cold gas vs a lot); environment (common in dense clusters vs in the field); surface brightness ($I\propto\exp[-7.67((r/r_e)^{1/4}-1)]$, de Vaucouleurs vs exponential disk $I_0e^{-r/r_d}$).

blocks.label: (9.4), (9.8). Measure a velocity, get the luminosity, compare with the flux: a distance.

blocks.html: Both scaling relations are the virial theorem in disguise: $v^2\sim GM/R$, and if all galaxies have similar surface brightness ($L/R^2$) and mass-to-light ratio, then $L\propto v^4$.
Spiral disks are bluer and younger than ellipticals (HS25 practice MC9). The bulges of spirals look like small ellipticals (old, red).

encounters.title: Synchrotron and bremsstrahlung: reading non-thermal and thermal light

blocks.html: Synchrotron: relativistic electrons spiralling around magnetic field lines. Relativistic beaming confines each electron's emission to a cone of angle $\sim1/\gamma$; the observer sees short pulses and the spectrum peaks near $ u\sim\gamma^2 u_g$, with $ u_g=eB/(2\pi m_e)=28\,\mathrm{GHz}\,(B/1\,\mathrm T)$. Two fingerprints. Synchrotron: power law, polarised, needs B and relativistic electrons (radio galaxies, supernova remnants, the Crab, the Galactic radio background). Bremsstrahlung: flat spectrum with an exponential cut-off at $h\nu\sim k_BT$ (so the cut-off measures $T$), unpolarised, $\propto n^2$ (two-body process). A cluster with $T=10^8$ K glows in X-rays ($k_BT\approx9$ keV), concentrated where the gas is densest.
Spectrum index sign: $p=2$ gives $f\propto\nu^{-1/2}$ (HS25 winter MC11), not $\nu^{-1}$. Bremsstrahlung goes as $\rho_{\rm gas}^2$, not $\rho$ (HS24 winter MC12).

blocks.html: Seyfert galaxies (1943): spirals with an unusually bright, point-like nucleus and strong emission lines (Seyfert 1: broad + narrow lines; Seyfert 2: only narrow). Radio galaxies: mostly ellipticals with giant radio lobes fed by jets. Quasars: the most luminous, often outshining the host 100×, seen to high redshift. Blazars: a jet pointing at us.

Size from variability: a source cannot vary coherently faster than light crosses it, $R\lesssim c\,\Delta t$. Quasars vary in days: $R\lesssim10^{-3}$ pc, smaller than the Solar System, yet $L\sim10^{39}$–$10^{40}$ W. Only accretion onto a supermassive black hole ($\eta\sim0.1$) delivers that: if $R\gtrsim r_s=2GM/c^2$, $M\lesssim Rc^2/2G$.

Unified model: a black hole with an accretion disk (thermal UV/optical "big blue bump"), fast clouds close in (broad lines), a dusty torus, slower clouds further out (narrow lines), and sometimes two jets. Seen face-on: Seyfert 1 / quasar; edge-on through the torus: Seyfert 2; down the jet: blazar.

blocks.label: Superluminal motion (9.21): a blob moving at v at angle θ to our line of sight.

blocks.html: Superluminal motion is a light-travel-time illusion: the blob almost catches up with its own light, so the arrival times are compressed while the sideways displacement is not. Nothing moves faster than $c$.

The Eddington limit caps the AGN luminosity: $L\le L_{Edd}=1.3\times10^{31}(M/M_\odot)$ W, which gives a lower limit on the black-hole mass, while variability gives an upper limit on the size and, via $r_s$, on the mass (HS24 winter Q6).

encounters.title: Clusters of galaxies and the cosmic web

blocks.html: A rich cluster: $\gtrsim100$ (up to thousands of) galaxies bound in a $\sim10^{15}M_\odot$ halo a few Mpc across. Mass budget: galaxies a few %, hot intracluster gas (ICM) ~15 %, dark matter ~80 %. Zwicky (1933) first found the "missing mass" from the virial theorem applied to the Coma cluster.

The ICM falls into the deep potential well and is shock-heated to the virial temperature, $k_BT\sim\mu m_p\sigma^2\approx10^8$ K for $\sigma\approx1000$ km/s: it shines in X-rays by bremsstrahlung. Scaling (HS25 winter Q5): $T\propto M/R\propto M^{2/3}$, $L_X\propto M^{4/3}$. It also scatters CMB photons to higher energy (Sunyaev–Zel'dovich effect). Gravitational lensing measures the total mass directly.

Three independent scales: galaxy velocities (virial), X-ray gas temperature (hydrostatic) and lensing (geometry) all give the same, dark-matter-dominated cluster mass. On larger scales galaxies form filaments, walls and voids (the cosmic web); only above $\sim100\,h^{-1}$ Mpc does the Universe look statistically homogeneous and isotropic (HS25 practice MC15).

encounters.title: Superluminal motion
encounters.goal: A blob moves at speed $v$ at angle $\theta$ to the line of sight towards us. Derive the apparent transverse speed $v_\perp$ and its maximum over $\theta$.

steps.prompt: Arrival times of signals emitted at A (t = 0) and at B (t = δt).
steps.reveal: $t_A=D/c$, $t_B=\delta t+(D-v\delta t\cos\theta)/c$, so $\Delta t_{\rm obs}=\delta t(1-\beta\cos\theta)$, $\beta=v/c$.

encounters.title: Three differences between spirals and ellipticals (exam explain question)
encounters.goal: Briefly explain three differences in the properties of spiral and elliptical galaxies, describing how each property is exhibited in both types.

steps.prompt: Write three on paper (2 pt each: name the property and state it for BOTH types). Then reveal a model list.
steps.reveal: Morphology (smooth ellipsoid vs disk with bulge, arms, bar); dynamics (random motions vs rotation of the disk); colour (red vs blue); stars (old, little star formation vs young, active star formation); gas (little cold gas vs much); environment (clusters vs field); clustering (stronger vs weaker); surface brightness ($r^{1/4}$ law vs exponential disk).

steps.prompt: Check that each of your answers says something about both types.
steps.reveal: "Ellipticals are red" alone is half an answer; "ellipticals are red because their stars are old, spirals are bluer because young massive stars are still forming in their gas-rich disks" is a full one.

encounters.title: Boss: quasar variability and black-hole mass (exam problem)
encounters.instructions: Solve on paper under the timer, then enter the final numbers.
statement: Quasars are often observed to exhibit variability with typical timescales on the order of a few days.

(a) [4 pt] Assuming variability of a quasar is observed on a characteristic timescale of 3 days, obtain an approximate limit on the length scale of the region responsible for this emission. How does this length scale compare to the typical size of a galaxy like the Milky Way?

(b) [4 pt] From the result of question (a), derive an approximate upper limit for the mass of the supermassive black hole which powers the AGN. Express your answer in solar masses. Hint: relate $D$ (the solution to part (a)) to the Schwarzschild radius.
keyPoints: (a) Causality: $D\lesssim c\Delta t=3\times10^5$ km/s $\times3\times86400$ s $=7.8\times10^{10}$ km $=2.5\times10^{-3}$ pc, about $10^{-7}$ of a 10 kpc galaxy.
